# Computing statistics









Computing population genetic statistics requires a specification of _what_
should be computed and _how_. Which individuals should a computation be
performed on? If multiple individuals should be grouped together, how do we
define these groups?

This chapter will teach you how to do this with _slendr_ by guiding you through
exercises focused on the most fundamental concepts of population genomics. The
focus will be less on teach you how these concepts work (you might be already be
quite familiar with) and more to give you the opportunity to learn the
technicalities of R and _slendr_ in a familiar context.

That said, the exercises have designed to provide interesting puzzles to
showcase the usefulness of simulation-based exploration even in (seemingly)
basic scenarios and applications, so that even readers relatively well familiar
with population genomics will appreciate a new perspective on familiar topics.











## Preparation


**Let's start with the following single-population model to keep things as
simple as possible. Look through the code to understand what it does, then save
it as `slendr_statistics_single.R`. Run the entire script and inspect the
produced visualization to make sure your understanding is correct.**

```{r}
#| output: false
#| collapse: true
library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = 5000)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = pop,
  generation_time = 1,
  simulation_length = 1000
)

plot_model(model)

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

samples <- ts_names(ts)
```












## Exercise: Adding mutations

When you typed `ts` in your R console earlier, you may have noticed a strange
thing --- although `msprime()` simulated genomic data, there are no mutations!
How can this be?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### See the `ts` summary

Here's the summary of the `ts` object simulated from the script above---notice
the "Mutations" field in the table below:

```{r}
ts
```

:::

As we will see later, the magic of tree sequences allows us to compute any
population genetic statistic without mutations. That said, particularly for
exploring statistics computed by various third-party software outside of R (and
for comparing simulations to these software methods), having mutations is often
useful. Here's how we can make that happen.

---

**Modify the part of your script `slendr_statistics_single.R` by "piping" the
output of the `msprime()` function to `ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)`
(remember the `%>%` "pipe operator" introduced in the earlier chapters). After
you execute this new command and type `ts` in the R console to inspect the
summary, you should see that mutations have been added.**
  
::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's the general pattern of how we simulate genomic data with _slendr_
including mutations:
  
```{r}
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

We can see that, indeed, the tree sequence now has `{r} ts$num_mutations`
mutations in it:
  
```{r}
ts
```

:::

Even though mutations are generally not needed, there's almost never any huge
downside to adding them, so I recommend you always use both `msprime()` and
`ts_mutate()` in your models.











## Exercise: Computing nucleotide diversity

The simplest possible computation we can do is to compute a statistic from a
single population. As an example, let's look at [nucleotide diversity
$\pi$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleotide_diversity), implemented by a
_slendr_ function `ts_diversity()`.

If you look at its help page under `?ts_diversity`, you will see that it accepts
several arguments---for now let's focus on the first two, `ts =` (which is
obviously a tree-sequence object, such as the one produced by the `msprime()`
engine) and `sample_sets =`.

**When you read the definition of [nucleotide
diversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleotide_diversity), knowing that
_slendr_ simulates diploids, how would you interpret the output of
`ts_diversity()` when you compute in on a single simulated individual, such as
the indivdual with the name "pop_1"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

The answer is that we get that individual's heterozygosity---the proportion of
their genome carrying heterozygous sites:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = "pop_1")
```

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- sum((ts_genotypes(ts)[, c("pop_1_chr1", "pop_1_chr2")] %>% rowSums()) == 1) / ts$sequence_length -->
<!-- ``` -->

Note that this is the same thing as the following command:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1"))
```

Because in R, a single value is the same thing as a vector of length one (this
might seem like a bit of curious trivia but it's good to keep in mind):

```{r}
"single_value" == c("single_value")

length(c("single_value"))
length("single_value")
```

:::

---

**Now run the following three commands. They look extremely similar, right? Do
they produce the same value? If not, how do you interpret them?**

(It turns out that patterns like these are very important for computing any kind
of tree-sequence statistic with _slendr_, so it very much pays off to think
about this, even though this looks trivial and nit-picky!)

```{r}
#| output: false
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_42"))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_42")))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

The first command is supposed to demonstrate that specifying a vector of
individuals' names to a statistic which operates within a given group of samples
simply computes that statistic as if each individual was its own sample:

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_2"))
```

The second command features the same vector of names, but wrapped in `list()`.
This is how you can instruct _slendr_ to treat a given set of individuals as
a group---and in this case, compute a statistic for the group as a whole. In this
context, this command computes the nucleotide diversity within the given sample
of two individuals from the whole population "pop":

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))
```

Notice that _slendr_ assigned this "anonymous" group of individuals the name "set_1".
Because these default names can be confusing in more complex computations of more
complex statistics, you can optionally specify the name of your group by providing
the set of individuals as a named list instead (see the R bootcamp chapter in case
you need a refresher on named lists and similar topics):

```{r}
ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(pop_subset = c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))
```

:::


---

The model which you programmed implies what should be the nucleotide diversity
expected in the simulated population. **Compute the nucleotide diversity in all
populations using `ts_diversity()`. Do you get numbers that (relatively between
all populations) match what would expect from the model you programmed?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = samples))
df
```

$\theta = 4 N_e \mu$

$N_e = \frac{\theta}{4 \mu}$

```{r}
df$Ne <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)

df
```

:::








## Exercise: Generalizing the simulation

Custom functions are absolutely critical for efficient, reproducible science.
They eliminate copy-pasted bug-prone code and make it much easier to explore
ideas, test parameters, and explore various models. In this workshop, you'll
soon see how often I force you to write custom functions---hopefully, by the end
you will appreciate why I did this!

To practice the concept of custom functions, let's start with something very easy.

Doing this work must seem like extra unnecessary bother. After all, you're
effectively writing _even more code_! But the pay off comes later, as you will
see.

The first instinct when a need to re-run an analysis with different parameters, or with different data, etc., is to just make a copy of your original script, and work from that, modifying the copied script and so on. This works, but is usually the wrong approach.

Let's first abstract away the computation of $\pi$ and the inference of $N_e$.
By extracting the relevant code into a dedicated, self-contained function, we
reduce duplication of code and, by extension, the potential for introducing
hard-to-trace bugs in our scripts.

```{r}
compute_pi <- function(model) {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  samples <- ts_names(ts)
  
  df <- ts_diversity(ts, list(all = samples))

  # compute the estimated Ne from the data based on the equation:
  #   theta = 4 * mutation_rate * Ne => Ne = theta / (4 * mutation_rate)
  df$Ne_estimated <- df$diversity / (4 * 1e-8)
  
  df
}
```

```{r}
compute_pi(model)
```

```{r}
simulate_const <- function(Ne) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = Ne)
  
  model <- compile_model(
    populations = pop,
    generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000
  )
  
  df <- compute_pi(model)

  # add annotation for downstream analyses
  df$Ne_true <- Ne

  df
}
```

```{r}
simulate_const(1000)
simulate_const(3000)
simulate_const(10000)
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

df_const <- map_dfr(c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000), simulate_const)

ggplot(df_const, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (constant model)")
```










## Exercise: Comparing multiple models

Let's suppose we want to see how robust our statistic of interest (in this toy
example, nucleotide divertisity, $\pi$) is to a choice of the underlying
demographic model. In the previous exercise, we worked with using $\pi$ to
estimate the effective population size of a population under study ($N_e$) and
verified that it works very well for a model of a long-term constant population size.

How about when we introduce a bottleneck into our model? How well does our $N_e$
estimate work in such case?

---

**Build a new model of a single population "pop", again starting with $N_e$ of
5000, then introduce a bottleneck using the function `resize()` which will set
the size of the population to the given value `Ne` at time 800. You can again
start by writing a couple of lines of code implementing such model, perhaps
setting the bottleneck to $N_e$ of 500, and once you have it, wrap it around in
a function `simulate_bottle(Ne)`, just like you did in the previous exercise.**

```{r}
pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = 5000) %>% resize(N = 500, time = 500)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = pop,
  generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

```{r}
simulate_bottle <- function(Ne) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = 5000) %>%  resize(N = Ne, time = 500)
  
  model <- compile_model(
    populations = pop,
    generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000
  )
  
  df <- compute_pi(model)

  # add annotation for downstream analyses
  df$Ne_true <- Ne

  df
}
```

We can see that even a drastic population bottleneck such as the one we
programmed does not actually reduce the observed levels of nucleotide diversity
that much! As a result, our $N_e$ estimate is very wrong---we consistently
estimate it at the level of 5000 (i.e., the size prior to the bottleneck),
regardless of the true size of the population after the bottleneck.

What this means that estimating $N_e$ from nucleotide diversity (which is very
often done in population genetics) only works reliably in a population which has
reached a long-term stable effective size.

We will see about a more robust method to do this in a later exercise.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

df_bottle <- map_dfr(c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000), simulate_bottle)

ggplot(df_bottle, aes(Ne_true, Ne_estimated)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5000, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggtitle("True Ne vs Ne estimated from nucleotide diversity (bottleneck model)") +
  ylim(0, 10000)
```















## Exercise: Allele frequency spectrum

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = 1000)
model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 20)

afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))

plot(afs, type = "l", col = "lightblue", xlab = "allele frequency", ylab = "count")
```

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

afs_const <- function(Ne) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = Ne)
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  data.frame(
    Ne = Ne,
    bin = 1:length(afs),
    freq = afs
  )
}
```

```{r}
afs <- map_dfr(c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000), afs_const)

ggplot(afs, aes(bin, freq, color = factor(Ne))) + geom_line()
```


```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

afs_bottle <- function(Ne) {
  pop <- population("pop", time = 1, N = 5000) %>%  resize(N = Ne, time = 500)
  model <- compile_model(populations = pop, generation_time = 1, simulation_length = 1000)
  
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), 10)
  
  afs <- ts_afs(ts, sample_sets = list(subset))
  
  data.frame(
    Ne = Ne,
    bin = 1:length(afs),
    freq = afs
  )
}
```

```{r}
afs <- map_dfr(c(1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000), afs_bottle)

ggplot(afs, aes(bin, freq, color = factor(Ne))) + geom_line()
```











## Exercise: Segregating sites and sequencing effort

Motivation: Single model, repeated computation on a subset of tree-sequence samples.

What if you wanted to get a good idea of a genetic diversity in your population,
or another summary statistic?

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 1000, N = 1000)
model <- compile_model(pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 20e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>% ts_mutate(1e-8)

ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = "pop_1")
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_2"))
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3"))

# oh no, a mistake, we forgot to group this
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = "pop_1"))
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = c("pop_1", "pop_2")))
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))

paste0("pop_", 1:3)

ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = paste0("pop_", 1:5)))

subset_segsites <- function(ts, i) {
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), i)

  df <- ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = subset))
  df$subset_n <- i

  df
}

subset_segsites(ts, 5)
```


```{r}
subset_n <- c(1:25, 50, 750, 100, 250, 500, 750, 1000)
subset_n

df <- map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_segsites(ts, .x))

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, segsites)) + geom_point()
```

```{r}
subset_n <- c(1:25, 50, 750, 100, 250, 500, 750, 1000)

subset_diversity <- function(ts, i) {
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), i)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(group = subset))
  df$subset_n <- i

  df
}

df <- map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x))

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point() + scale_x_continuous()

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point() + scale_x_log10()
```


```{r}
df <- rbind(
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x))
)

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + scale_x_continuous()

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + scale_x_log10()

ggplot(df, aes(factor(subset_n), diversity)) + geom_boxplot()
```







## Bonus exercise: Your own model

If you got all the way here while the others are still working on their solutions,
here's a bonus exercise for you.

**Take a demographic model of an organism or a population which is of your
interest in your own research (either your own model or a model you know from
the literature) and program it with _slendr_. Feel free to be as detailed (or
not) as possible, but don't worry about accuracy of various parameters. The
point is to practice building a model from scratch. Then, compute the basic
summary statistics introduced in this chapter on simulations from your model. Do
the results match what you know, either from your research or from the
literature? If not, what could be the problem?**

If these statistics aren't particularly interesting or relevant for your
research, don't despair. Again, the point is to practice, but even then, you'll
have plenty of opportunities to compute more interesting things throughout this
course, particularly during the "freeform" sessions at the very end.
